entries.meaning: The contraction of I will. Besides the plain future it carries the use Russian speakers most often lose — a decision made at the moment of speaking. The phone rings and an American says I'll get it, where Russian uses a present-tense perfective (я открою); learners produce ✗ I get it, which sounds like a statement of habit. ---
examples: Someone's at the door — I'll get it.
I'll be thirty in March.
Text me when you land and I'll come pick you up.
entries.русский: я буду, я сделаю — сокращение от I will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: I'll is an exact homophone of aisle and isle; only the spelling separates them. And no contraction may end a clause: the answer to Will you come? is I will, never ✗ I'll.

entries.meaning: The contraction of you will, singular or plural. ---
examples: You'll need a passport, not just a driver's license.
If you leave now, you'll miss the worst of the traffic.
Don't worry — you'll get used to it.
entries.русский: ты будешь, вы будете — сокращение от you will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.question form: Will you help me? — 'll never inverts, so the question puts the full will in front of the subject. There is no ✗ 'll you help me?; You'll help me? exists only as a surprised echo, said with rising intonation.
entries.contrast: You'll and yule (as in yule log) are homophones, both /juːl/. In fast speech it reduces further, to /jəl/, so You'll see comes out as 'yuhl-SEE' — the whole future is one unstressed /l/.

examples: He'll be back on Monday.
Ask Daniel — he'll know how the filing system works.
I doubt he'll remember me.
entries.русский: он будет, он сделает — сокращение от he will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: He'll is an exact homophone of heal and heel, and the vowel has to stay long: with the short vowel of bed you have said hell. After another word the /h/ usually drops, so when he'll be back runs together as 'when-EEL'.

examples: She'll be here around seven.
Give Priya the file and she'll take it from there.
I don't think she'll mind.
entries.русский: она будет, она сделает — сокращение от she will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: Keep the vowel long — she'll has the vowel of see; the short vowel of bed gives shell. In fast speech the contraction can shrink to a syllabic /l/, so She'll call you is often just 'shl-CALL-you' and the future is easy to miss.

entries.meaning: The contraction of it will. It is one of the commonest things an American says and one of the rarest to see printed — in a report or a cover letter it is spelled out. ---
examples: Don't worry — it'll be fine.
It'll take about twenty minutes to get downtown.
If you leave the milk out, it'll go bad.
entries.русский: оно будет, это будет — сокращение от it will
entries.register: informal — everywhere in speech, but rare on the page outside dialogue, email, and text messages
entries.contrast: The /t/ flaps, so it'll is two syllables that sound like 'IH-duhl', close to it all. Stress tells them apart: it all leans on all, it'll leans on it. In anything formal, write it will.

examples: We'll let you know by Friday.
If the weather holds, we'll eat outside.
We'll have been married ten years this June.
entries.русский: мы будем, мы сделаем — сокращение от we will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: We'll is an exact homophone of wheel; American English lost the old wh- sound. The trap is length: the vowel is long, and shortening it turns we'll into will, so We'll see is heard as will see, which is not a sentence.

examples: They'll be here by six.
Ask the neighbors — they'll know when the truck comes.
I doubt they'll agree to that price.
entries.русский: они будут, они сделают — сокращение от they will
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: They'll and there'll sound close but do different work: they'll points back to people or things already named, while there'll introduces something new (There'll be trouble). The possessive their never contracts — ✗ their'll does not exist.

entries.meaning: The contraction of there will, almost always in front of be: it is the future of there is and there are. Like those, it takes its number from what follows rather than from there — there'll be one chair, there'll be ten chairs. ---
examples: There'll be about forty people at the wedding.
There'll always be someone who complains.
I don't think there'll be enough chairs.
entries.русский: будет, будут (в обороте there will be) — сокращение от there will
entries.register: standard — ordinary in speech and in most writing; the full form is only needed where the sentence wants weight
entries.contrast: Not the possessive: their never takes 'll, and ✗ their'll is not a word. In running speech there'll is barely distinguishable from they'll, and only the sense sorts them out.

entries.meaning: The contraction of that will. Two fixed phrases carry much of its work: that'll do means 'enough, stop there', and that'll be the day is sarcasm — it says the thing will never happen. A cashier's that'll be fourteen dollars is the plain future being polite. ---
examples: That'll be fourteen dollars even.
That'll do — we don't need any more chairs.
Marcus, apologize? That'll be the day.
entries.русский: это будет, этого хватит — сокращение от that will
entries.register: informal — common in speech, above all in fixed phrases; rare in formal writing
entries.contrast: The /t/ flaps, so that'll is two syllables: 'THAD-uhl'. Keep that'll do ('that is enough, stop') apart from that'll do it ('that finishes the job') — both are everyday, and they are not the same remark.

entries.meaning: The contraction of who will, in questions and in reported questions. ---
examples: Who'll drive us to the airport?
We still don't know who'll be running the meeting.
Who'll go first?
entries.русский: кто будет — сокращение от who will
entries.register: standard — ordinary in speech and in most writing; the full form is only needed where the sentence wants weight
entries.question form: Who'll drive? — who is the subject, so nothing inverts and the contraction survives inside the question, unlike you'll, which has to open out into Will you…?
entries.contrast: Who'll rhymes with cool, not with whole — it is not a homophone of whole or hole.

examples: What'll happen if I press this?
What'll you have to drink?
What'll it take to get this done today?
entries.русский: что будет, что сделает — сокращение от what will
entries.register: informal — speech and written dialogue only; formal writing keeps what will
entries.question form: What'll you have? — with what as the object, will still inverts with the subject, but the 'll rides on what, not on you: never ✗ What you'll have?
entries.contrast: The /t/ flaps, so what'll is a near-homophone of waddle: What'll I do? arrives as 'WAH-dul-eye-doo'. That is why learners miss the question's future entirely — the whole of will is one unstressed syllable.
